newsitem.title: JAPAN: Alaskan crude losing lustre with Japan's traders.
newsitem.headline: Alaskan crude losing lustre with Japan's traders.

text.p: Alaska North Slope (ANS) crude oil has lost some of its initial appeal with Japanese refiners, oil traders said on Friday.

Nearly a year has passed since lead Alaskan oil producer British Petroleum Co Plc began experimental shipments of the sour Alaskan grade to the growing Asian market following the lifting of a U.S. export ban.
"At current prices, ANS is not an attractive option for us, and there is a growing concern with the grade's quality," said one buyer.

Japan's Idemitsu Kosan Co Ltd and Cosmo Oil Co Ltd were among the first customers in the region to sample the grade as a possible alternative to sour Mideast benchmarks Oman and Dubai, but traders now suggest any future term contract arrangements between Japanese majors and marketers of the Alaskan sour grade are unlikely.

While some crude oil dealers say the competitiveness of ANS against its Middle Eastern counterparts is a simple issue of price, others cite quality issues like high metal content, problematic cetane levels and a low middle-distillate yield.

One trader with a Japanese refiner noted a growing concern among buyers over reports in a trade journal that a major South Korean customer had suspended purchases of ANS due to quality problems in a recent spot cargo.
"We have heard reports that high alkaline levels led to problems in the secondary units of some Korean refiners," the trader said.
ANS is a heavy, 29.5 degree API (American Petroleum Institute) gravity crude with a sulphur content of 1.05 percent.
Idemitsu, which imported 1.3 million barrels of ANS crude last August, says that it has not noted any quality shortfalls, and will consider the Alaskan grade on a spot basis when prices allow.
"We have not made further purchases because BP has not approached us recently, but quality has not been a factor for us," a company spokesman said.
March deliveries of ANS to Asia were estimated by one BP analyst to be 100,000 to 120,000 barrels per day (bpd) out of Valdez.
That represents nearly a 10th of total ANS production and a 60,000 to 80,000 bpd gain over levels seen in the first months of the BP export programme.

BP is one of several major oil companies, including the state National Iranian Oil Company, Norway's Statoil and the state Nigerian National Oil Company, which are focusing their marketing efforts on the burgeoning Asian energy market.
The British company has also been promoting future sales of Alaskan liquefied natural gas (LNG). North Slope LNG production and exports are expected to start by 2007.
Japan, the world's largest LNG buyer, imported 43 million tonnes of LNG in 1995, accounting for about 63 percent of all LNG cargoes traded on the international market in that year.
